queue.title: Semiconductor Supply Resilience: Diversification
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses semiconductor supply resilience, key risks, and practical consequences for manufacturers.

Dependence on a single semiconductor component manufacturer exposes a company to risk beyond its own control over production.

Global concentration of advanced semiconductor component manufacturing in a small number of geographic locations creates systemic risk that an individual company can't eliminate, only manage.

Geopolitical tensions, natural disasters, or a simple surge in demand can simultaneously hit all customers dependent on the same manufacturer, regardless of individual contract size.

Qualifying alternative suppliers for critical components, even at a higher unit price, acts as insurance against a complete production halt at the moment of a supply disruption.

Strategic stockpiles of critical components, though they tie up working capital, can be a justified cost compared to the price of a complete production stoppage due to unavailability of one component.

queue.title: Payment Infrastructure Resilience
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses payment infrastructure resilience, key risks, and practical consequences for companies.

A company dependent on a single payment channel carries an operational risk comparable to dependence on a single electricity supplier.

An outage at one bank, payment processor, or clearing system, however brief, directly halts a company's ability to pay suppliers or receive customer payments.

Diversifying payment channels — multiple banking relationships, alternative processors for critical transactions — reduces that exposure in a way similar to raw-material supplier diversification.

Testing scenarios of temporary unavailability of the primary payment channel, including a clear plan for who approves an alternative payment path, is rarely part of a standard business continuity plan.

The cost of maintaining an alternative payment channel is almost always lower than the cost of several days of operational downtime when the primary channel is unavailable.

queue.title: Operational Resilience and Business Continuity
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses operational resilience, key frameworks, and practical consequences for business continuity.

Business continuity requires clear priorities, replacement processes, and regular testing of decisions before an actual disruption.

Operational resilience doesn't begin with a crisis plan but with understanding the processes without which an organisation can't deliver core value.

A practical framework links critical processes, responsible people, backup suppliers, and acceptable recovery time.

Regular scenario testing reveals assumptions that most often become failure points in an actual disruption.
